definition: Statistical shape analysis is an analysis of the geometrical properties of some given set of shapes by statistical methods.
details: For instance, it could be used to quantify differences between male and female gorilla skull shapes, normal and pathological bone shapes, leaf outlines with and without herbivory by insects, etc. Important aspects of shape analysis are to obtain a measure of distance between shapes, to estimate mean shapes from (possibly random) samples, to estimate shape variability within samples, to perform clustering and to test for differences between shapes. One of the main methods used is principal component analysis (PCA). Statistical shape analysis has applications in various fields, including medical imaging, computer vision, computational anatomy, sensor measurement, and geographical profiling.

explainer.lead: Statistical shape analysis applies statistical methods to the geometric properties of sets of shapes. It matters because it turns shape differences into quantities that can be compared, averaged, clustered and tested.

tiers.eli5: You line up a batch of outlines — say, skulls or leaves — and measure how each one bends away from the average, so you can tell which differences are real.
tiers.practitioner: Analysts need a distance measure between shapes, mean shapes from samples, and variability estimates before clustering or testing. A pitfall is that results depend heavily on how shapes are aligned and represented.
tiers.paperLevel: Core tasks are a distance measure between shapes, estimation of mean shapes from possibly random samples, estimation of within-sample shape variability, clustering, and tests for differences between shapes. Principal component analysis is one of the main methods used.

explainer.example: Comparing male and female gorilla skull shapes, or leaf outlines with and without insect herbivory, by quantifying differences and testing whether they are significant.
